opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm uncertain, but I'd push back on treating it as a slam dunk. The basic argument is intuitive: if AI makes AI researchers ten times more productive, you get better AI faster, which makes researchers even more productive, and you get a feedback loop that runs away from you. I think the loop is real. The question is whether it's accelerating or whether it fizzles out, and that depends on details that people often skip over.

The first thing I'd ask is: ten times more productive at *what*? A lot of AI progress, at least historically, has come from compute. You scale up the model, scale up the data, and capabilities improve. If your researchers get ten times faster at writing code and having ideas, but you're still bottlenecked on how many GPUs you have and how long a training run takes, you don't get anything like a 10x speedup in overall progress. It's an Amdahl's law situation. You speed up the parts of the pipeline you can speed up, and the parts you can't speed up come to dominate. So I'd want to know what fraction of progress is really researcher-labor-limited versus compute-limited.

The second thing is diminishing returns to research. Ideas get harder to find. There's decent economic evidence that across many fields you need exponentially more research effort to sustain the same rate of progress. So the real question for an intelligence explosion is a race: does each improvement in AI boost research productivity by more than the increase in difficulty of the next improvement? If yes, you get explosive dynamics. If no, you get a one-time boost, maybe a big one, and then things settle back toward a faster but not runaway trajectory. I don't think anyone has a confident estimate of which side of that line we're on. People have tried to estimate it, and the answers tend to land uncomfortably close to the threshold, which is part of why I take it seriously.

The third thing is that "ten times more productive" is doing a lot of work. Making each researcher 10x faster is very different from having a million copies of a top researcher running in parallel at 50x speed. If you get to the second regime, where AIs are doing basically all of the research themselves, the compute bottleneck still matters, but you can use that labor in clever ways, like running smaller experiments, getting more out of each training run, or improving algorithms so you need less compute. Algorithmic progress has been a substantial share of overall gains, so a big surge in research labor could matter a lot even if compute stays fixed.

So where do I come out? I think "10x productivity automatically means an intelligence explosion" is too strong. Bottlenecks and diminishing returns are real, and I'd guess the first stages of AI-assisted research look more like a substantial acceleration than a discontinuity. But I also don't think you can confidently rule out a fast takeoff, especially once you're past the point where AIs are mostly augmenting humans and are doing most of the research. And from a safety perspective, that's the part that matters. Even if the probability is moderate, a world where progress compresses dramatically is one where our ability to notice problems, iterate on alignment techniques, and coordinate gets squeezed. So I'd rather we prepare for the faster scenario than bet on the bottlenecks saving us.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I find it plausible but much less automatic than the way it's usually framed.

So the argument as it's typically stated goes something like: right now AI progress is bottlenecked on a few thousand researchers at the top labs. If you can make each of them ten times as productive, that's like having ten times as many researchers, progress speeds up, which makes the AI better, which makes the researchers even more productive, and you get this feedback loop that runs away. And I think every individual step there is somewhat true, but the conclusion depends a lot on details that people tend to skip over.

The first thing I'd push on is what "ten times more productive" actually means. If you mean that researchers can write code ten times faster, that's a very different thing from being ten times better at generating good research ideas, or ten times better at figuring out which experiments are worth running. In my experience, a lot of the actual bottleneck in research isn't the typing. It's taste. It's knowing which of the fifty things you could try is the one that's going to matter. And it's not obvious to me that current systems help much with that, or that making coding faster translates into making that part faster.

The second thing is compute. Even if you had infinitely many brilliant researchers with perfect ideas, you still have to run the experiments, and the experiments take GPUs and time. If the binding constraint is that you can only run so many large training runs per month, then speeding up the humans gives you diminishing returns pretty quickly. You end up with a lot of very fast people waiting in line for the cluster. Now, you could argue that smarter researchers would use compute more efficiently, and I think that's partly true, but it's a much weaker effect than a straightforward ten-x.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most important, is that "ten times more productive" is a snapshot, and the intelligence explosion argument needs a rate. It needs that each round of improvement produces a next round that's at least as big, and keeps doing so. It's entirely consistent with the evidence to think you get a one-time boost, a big jump, and then you're back to progress being bounded by the things that were always hard: data, compute, physical experiments, the fact that some problems just take a long time to think through even if you think fast.

So where I actually land is: I think a big acceleration in AI research from AI assistance is quite likely. I think that's one of the main reasons timelines might be shorter than people expected. But I'm pretty uncertain whether that turns into the classic runaway dynamic, and I'd put real weight on scenarios where you get something more like a few years of unusually fast progress rather than weeks or months of a system rapidly bootstrapping itself. And honestly, from a safety perspective, the difference between those two worlds matters enormously, because a few years is something institutions can plausibly react to, and a few weeks isn't. So I'd want people to hold both possibilities rather than treating the explosion as the default outcome of productivity gains.

astra-6.text:
I think it would be a big deal, but I don’t think an intelligence explosion follows just from that. There’s a distinction between making research much faster and creating a feedback loop that keeps accelerating.

Suppose you make AI researchers ten times more productive. They develop the next generation of AI faster. The question is: how much better is that next generation at doing AI research? Does it give you another comparable increase in productivity, and can you keep repeating that? Or have you picked the low-hanging fruit, so the next improvement takes substantially more work?

You also have to ask what’s actually being sped up. If researchers can come up with ideas and write code ten times faster, but still have to wait for training runs and experiments, then the whole research process isn’t necessarily ten times faster. Compute or the time it takes to build more hardware could become the bottleneck.

So I’d take that as a reason to expect potentially very rapid progress. But to conclude that you get an intelligence explosion, you need additional assumptions about the returns to research and how those bottlenecks change as AI improves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would be a big deal, but I don’t think an intelligence explosion follows automatically. There’s a difference between making researchers ten times more productive and making the entire process of improving AI ten times faster. Researchers still need to run experiments, acquire compute, and wait for results. If you speed up one part of that process, some other part becomes the bottleneck.

Then there’s the question of what happens on the next round. Suppose AI helps us build a better AI system. Does that system make research another ten times more productive, or does it take us from ten times to eleven times? Both are compatible with the initial claim, but they imply very different trajectories.

So I’d want to understand the strength of that feedback loop. How much better does the next system get, how much does that improvement help with research, and how quickly can you turn the research into another deployed system? Ten times more productive is evidence that we could see substantial acceleration. By itself, it doesn’t establish a runaway process.
